about: Lifestyle Medicine and Prevention Year 1 (MEDI40005) is a core 10-credit module running from autumn to summer of Year 1 at Imperial (2026-27 programme specification). Imperial's School of Public Health describes this first-year part of LMAP (LMAP-1A) as covering core lifestyle factors, their effect on health and behaviour change theory using COM-B, taught mostly online through a flipped-classroom design with clinician-led small-group tutorials. On those pages (last updated 2022), assessment is a Term 3 group audio podcast on one lifestyle theme, worth 80% of the mark, with an individual academic commentary and peer evaluation making up the rest; check the current module handbook for any changes. Topics follow the order on the module's About page.

notes.body:
Lifestyle medicine depends on judging evidence about behaviour and health, much of which comes from observational studies. This topic gives you the tools to read that evidence critically and the ethical rules for research on people.

The scientific method
- Observe, form a testable hypothesis, make a prediction, test it, then revise.
- Karl Popper (The Logic of Scientific Discovery; German original 1934) argued that scientific claims must be falsifiable: a good hypothesis states what result would prove it wrong.

Study designs (roughly from weaker to stronger evidence for cause and effect)
- Case reports and series: describe; generate hypotheses.
- Cross-sectional surveys: measure exposure and outcome at one time; good for prevalence, weak on direction of cause.
- Case–control studies: compare past exposures of people with and without a disease; efficient for rare diseases; give an odds ratio; prone to recall bias.
- Cohort studies: follow exposed and unexposed people forward; give relative risk; can study several outcomes.
- Randomised controlled trials (RCTs): randomisation balances known and unknown confounders, so differences can be attributed to the intervention.
- Systematic reviews and meta-analyses: pool all relevant studies using explicit methods.

Why lifestyle evidence is hard
- Confounding: a third factor linked to both exposure and outcome. For example, people who exercise may also smoke less and earn more.
- Reverse causation: illness may cause the "exposure" (people who are unwell may become less active).
- Bias: selection bias (who takes part) and information bias (e.g. inaccurate recall of diet).
- Bradford Hill (1965) suggested viewpoints for judging causation: strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient (dose–response), plausibility, coherence, experiment and analogy. Only temporality (cause before effect) is essential.

Measuring effects: worked example
In a trial, 10% of the control group and 6% of the intervention group have a heart attack.
- Relative risk (RR) = 0.06 / 0.10 = 0.6.
- Relative risk reduction = (0.10 − 0.06) / 0.10 = 40%.
- Absolute risk reduction = 10% − 6% = 4 percentage points.
- Number needed to treat = 1 / 0.04 = 25.
Relative figures sound larger than absolute ones; patients need both to make an informed decision.

Statistical significance is not the same as importance. A p-value below 0.05 is a convention, not proof; confidence intervals show the range of plausible effect sizes and are more informative.

Research ethics
- The Nuremberg Code (1947) followed the trial of Nazi doctors and made voluntary consent essential.
- The World Medical Association's Declaration of Helsinki (first adopted 1964, most recently revised in October 2024) sets out principles for medical research involving people.
- The Tuskegee syphilis study (1932–1972), in which treatment was withheld from Black men without their informed consent, led in the United States to the Belmont Report (1979), with its principles of respect for persons, beneficence and justice.
- Core requirements today: informed, voluntary consent; the right to withdraw; confidentiality; a favourable balance of risk and benefit; fair selection of participants; and approval by an independent research ethics committee (in the UK, through the NHS research ethics system overseen in England by the Health Research Authority).
- LMAP itself has used this in practice: the module pages (last updated 2022) describe an optional Lifestyle Tracking Study in which students could choose to share smartphone activity data for analysis.

Exam tips: calculate both relative and absolute measures, name a specific confounder rather than just saying "confounding", and link each ethical principle to the event that shaped it.

Population health looks at the health of whole groups and the factors that shape it, many of which lie outside healthcare.

Determinants of health
Dahlgren and Whitehead's "rainbow" model (1991) places the individual (age, sex, genes) at the centre, surrounded by layers of influence:
- Individual lifestyle factors (smoking, diet, activity).
- Social and community networks.
- Living and working conditions (education, work, housing, healthcare, water and sanitation, food).
- General socio-economic, cultural and environmental conditions.
The point is that behaviour sits inside social and economic circumstances that make healthy choices easier or harder.

Health inequalities
- Health inequalities are systematic, avoidable and unfair differences in health between groups.
- The social gradient: health tends to improve step by step with each rise in social position, not just between the poorest and everyone else. The Black Report (1980) documented this in Britain.
- The Marmot Review, "Fair Society, Healthy Lives" (2010), argued for action across the life course and for proportionate universalism: universal action, with scale and intensity proportionate to need.
- "Health Equity in England: The Marmot Review 10 Years On" (2020) reported that improvement in life expectancy had stalled, that inequalities had widened, and that life expectancy had fallen for women in the most deprived areas.
- The inverse care law (Julian Tudor Hart, Lancet, 1971): the availability of good medical care tends to vary inversely with the need for it in the population served.
- NHS England's Core20PLUS5 approach targets healthcare inequalities in the most deprived 20% of the population plus other locally identified groups.

Two strategies of prevention (Geoffrey Rose)
In "Sick individuals and sick populations" (1985) Rose distinguished:
- The high-risk strategy: find and treat individuals at high risk. Well targeted and motivating for those individuals, but it misses most cases and does not change the underlying causes.
- The population strategy: shift the whole distribution of a risk factor (e.g. reducing salt in processed food). It addresses root causes but offers little benefit to each individual.
The prevention paradox: a measure that brings large benefits to the population may offer little to each participating individual. Worked example: 90% of a population are low risk (1% develop disease) and 10% are high risk (5% develop disease). Cases from the low-risk group = 0.9 × 0.01 = 0.009; from the high-risk group = 0.1 × 0.05 = 0.005. So about 64% of cases (0.009 / 0.014) come from the low-risk majority.

Levels of prevention
- Primary: stop disease starting (vaccination, smoking cessation).
- Secondary: detect early to improve outcome (screening, e.g. cervical screening).
- Tertiary: reduce complications of established disease (cardiac rehabilitation).
Wilson and Jungner's screening principles (WHO, 1968) include that the condition is an important health problem, there is a recognisable early stage, an acceptable test and an effective treatment.

Key measures
- Incidence: new cases in a population over a period. Prevalence: all existing cases at a point or period.
- Life expectancy versus healthy life expectancy: the gap between deprived and affluent areas is larger for healthy life expectancy.

Exam tips: use the rainbow model to structure answers about causes, give Rose's two strategies with an example of each, and be able to explain the prevention paradox with numbers.

LMAP-1A is built around individual behaviour change, and the module pages name COM-B as the framework students use. Expect to apply it to real behaviours.

The COM-B model
Michie, van Stralen and West (2011) proposed that behaviour (B) results from the interaction of three components:
- Capability: physical (skills, strength) and psychological (knowledge, memory, attention).
- Opportunity: physical (time, money, environment, access) and social (norms, culture, support).
- Motivation: reflective (plans, beliefs, intentions) and automatic (habits, emotions, impulses).
Changing behaviour means identifying which components are lacking and targeting them.

The Behaviour Change Wheel
COM-B sits at the centre of the Behaviour Change Wheel, which links it to:
- Nine intervention functions: education, persuasion, incentivisation, coercion, training, restriction, environmental restructuring, modelling and enablement.
- Seven policy categories: communication/marketing, guidelines, fiscal measures, regulation, legislation, environmental/social planning and service provision.

Behaviour change techniques (BCTs)
The BCT Taxonomy v1 (Michie and colleagues, 2013) lists 93 techniques in 16 groups, giving a shared language for what interventions contain. Commonly used ones:
- Goal setting (behaviour or outcome) and action planning (when, where, how).
- Self-monitoring of behaviour (e.g. step counts) and feedback on behaviour.
- Prompts and cues; habit formation (repeating the behaviour in the same context).
- Social support (practical or emotional).
- Problem solving: identifying barriers and planning around them.
Habits take time: in a study by Lally and colleagues (2010), the median time for a new daily behaviour to become automatic was 66 days, with a very wide range (18 to 254 days).

Other models you should know
- Health Belief Model (1950s): action depends on perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers and cues to action, and self-efficacy.
- Theory of Planned Behaviour (Ajzen, 1991): intention is shaped by attitudes, subjective norms and perceived behavioural control.
- Transtheoretical (stages of change) model (Prochaska and DiClemente): precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance, with relapse common. It is widely taught, but evidence that stage-matched interventions work better than others is mixed, so it is contested as a basis for designing interventions.

UK guidance
NICE public health guideline PH49, "Behaviour change: individual approaches" (published January 2014; a 2019 surveillance review decided no update was needed), recommends that interventions use proven techniques such as goal setting, planning, self-monitoring, feedback and social support, and that staff delivering them are trained. Making Every Contact Count encourages health professionals to use routine contacts for brief conversations about health.

Worked example: COM-B diagnosis
A student wants to walk to campus but keeps taking the bus.
- Capability: knows the route? Is fit enough?
- Opportunity: is there time in the morning; is the route safe; do friends walk?
- Motivation: does she value it (reflective); is taking the bus automatic (habit)?
If the main barrier is time and habit, useful BCTs are action planning (leave 20 minutes earlier on set days), prompts (a phone reminder) and habit formation, rather than more education.

Exam tips: diagnose before prescribing: identify the COM-B components first, then choose intervention functions and specific named BCTs that match them.

These three themes are linked: poor sleep and chronic stress affect health directly and also make dependence on substances more likely, and vice versa.

Sleep
- Structure: non-REM sleep (stages N1–N3, with N3 being deep slow-wave sleep) alternates with REM sleep in cycles of roughly 90 minutes. Slow-wave sleep is concentrated early in the night, REM later.
- The two-process model (Borbély, 1982): Process S, a homeostatic sleep pressure that builds while awake (adenosine is one contributor), and Process C, the circadian rhythm.
- The circadian clock is the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus. Light reaching the retina entrains it via the retinohypothalamic tract; in darkness the pineal gland releases melatonin.
- How much? NHS advice is that most adults need about 7 to 9 hours a night.
- Effects of insufficient sleep: impaired attention, memory and mood, and more errors and accidents. Short sleep is associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease; these links are largely observational, though experimental sleep restriction shows short-term effects such as reduced insulin sensitivity.
- Management: regular sleep and wake times, light exposure in the morning, limiting caffeine and alcohol, and a dark, quiet bedroom. For long-term insomnia, cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the recommended first-line treatment in UK guidance.

Stress
- A stressor is any demand; the stress response depends on how it is appraised. Lazarus and Folkman's transactional model (1984) describes primary appraisal (is this a threat?) and secondary appraisal (can I cope?).
- Physiology: the fast sympathetic–adrenal medullary response (adrenaline and noradrenaline) and the slower HPA axis (CRH → ACTH → cortisol), with cortisol feeding back negatively.
- Acute stress can improve performance up to a point; very high arousal impairs it (the inverted-U idea often credited to Yerkes and Dodson, 1908).
- Allostatic load (McEwen and Stellar, 1993) describes the cumulative "wear and tear" from repeated or prolonged activation of stress systems.
- Healthy coping: problem-focused coping where the problem can be changed, emotion-focused coping and social support where it cannot; adequate sleep and activity.

Dependence
- ICD-11 defines substance dependence by three features: impaired control over use; use taking increasing priority over other activities; and physiological features (tolerance, withdrawal, or using to avoid withdrawal). Two of the three are usually needed over at least 12 months (or at least 3 months if use is continuous, daily or almost daily).
- Neurobiology: drugs of dependence increase dopamine in the mesolimbic reward pathway (ventral tegmental area to nucleus accumbens), reinforcing use; tolerance and withdrawal reflect adaptation.
- ICD-11 also recognises gambling disorder and gaming disorder as behavioural addictions.

Alcohol
- UK Chief Medical Officers' low-risk drinking guidelines (2016): to keep health risks low it is safest for men and women not to drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, spread over three or more days; if pregnant or planning pregnancy, the safest approach is not to drink at all.
- One UK unit is 10 mL (8 g) of pure alcohol. Units = volume (mL) × ABV (%) ÷ 1,000. A 500 mL can at 5% = 2.5 units; a 175 mL glass of wine at 12% = 2.1 units; a 750 mL bottle at 13.5% ≈ 10 units.
- Screening: the WHO's AUDIT questionnaire (10 items) and its short form AUDIT-C.

Tobacco and nicotine
Smoking remains a leading preventable cause of illness and death. Combining behavioural support with stop-smoking medicines gives the best quit rates. NICE guideline NG209 (2021) includes nicotine-containing e-cigarettes as an option for adults trying to quit; their long-term effects are still uncertain and how strongly to promote them is debated.

Exam tips: show unit calculations, describe dependence with the ICD-11 features, and connect stress physiology to sleep and substance use.

Social relationships are a determinant of health in their own right, comparable in size to some well-known risk factors. This theme also covers how relationships can harm health.

The evidence
- Holt-Lunstad, Smith and Layton (PLoS Medicine, 2010) pooled 148 studies with over 300,000 participants and found that people with stronger social relationships had about a 50% greater likelihood of survival over the follow-up period (odds ratio about 1.5).
- These are observational data, so confounding and reverse causation (illness reducing social contact) cannot be fully excluded, but the association is consistent across many studies.
- Terms: social isolation is an objective lack of contact; loneliness is the subjective feeling that one's relationships are inadequate. They overlap but are not the same, and each is linked with poorer health.

How relationships affect health: proposed mechanisms
- Stress buffering (Cohen and Wills, 1985): support reduces the impact of stressors, dampening HPA and sympathetic responses.
- Main (direct) effect: being integrated in a network benefits health regardless of stress, e.g. through a sense of purpose and belonging.
- Health behaviours: networks shape norms about smoking, drinking, eating and activity, and partners and friends can encourage help-seeking and adherence to treatment.
- Physiology: loneliness is associated with raised blood pressure, inflammation and disturbed sleep.
- Claims that conditions such as obesity "spread" through social networks (Christakis and Fowler, 2007) were influential but contested on methodological grounds.

Policy in the UK
In 2018 the UK government appointed its first minister with responsibility for loneliness and published its first loneliness strategy, "A connected society". Social prescribing, in which link workers connect patients to community groups and activities, is part of NHS personalised care and is covered further in LMAP-1B.

When relationships harm
- Domestic abuse is a major cause of physical and mental ill health. In England and Wales, the Domestic Abuse Act 2021 created a statutory definition that includes physical, sexual, economic, psychological and emotional abuse and controlling or coercive behaviour, between people aged 16 or over who are personally connected.
- Health professionals should be alert to signs, ask about abuse when the person is alone and safe to talk, and know local referral routes.
- Adverse childhood experiences (such as abuse, neglect and household dysfunction) are associated with poorer adult health and more risk behaviours.

Relationships in practice
- For patients: asking "who is around to support you?" is part of a full social history and of planning care.
- For you: medical training can strain relationships; keeping up friendships and support networks protects your own wellbeing.
- The doctor–patient relationship itself matters; trust and continuity support honest discussion of lifestyle.

Exam tips: distinguish isolation from loneliness, explain at least two mechanisms, and say clearly that most evidence is observational when discussing causation.

Money affects health through material conditions, stress and access to opportunities, and ill health can in turn damage finances. LMAP treats financial wellbeing as a lifestyle theme for both patients and students.

What is financial wellbeing?
The Money and Pensions Service, which leads the UK Strategy for Financial Wellbeing (2020–2030), describes it in terms of feeling secure and in control: managing day to day, being able to cope with unexpected costs and being on track for the future. It is about control and security, not just income.

Income, poverty and health
- Income is a core social determinant of health and follows the social gradient: health improves step by step with rising income.
- Pathways from low income to poor health:
  - Material: poor-quality or cold housing, food insecurity, less access to healthy food and safe places to exercise.
  - Psychosocial: chronic stress, insecurity and lack of control, with effects on sleep and mental health.
  - Behavioural: smoking and some other risk behaviours are more common in deprived groups, often as coping strategies.
- Cold homes: NICE guideline NG6 (2015) addresses the health risks of cold homes and excess winter deaths, recognising fuel poverty as a health issue.

Debt and mental health
- Problem debt is strongly associated with depression and anxiety, and people with mental health problems are more likely to be in problem debt.
- The relationship runs both ways: illness can reduce earnings and make money management harder, and debt causes stress. Most evidence is observational, so the size of the causal effect in each direction is uncertain.
- Debt is also linked to suicidal thoughts, so asking about money worries is part of a good risk assessment.

Practical help
- Ask: "Are money worries affecting your health?" is a simple, acceptable question in many consultations.
- Signpost: free, independent debt advice (e.g. Citizens Advice and debt advice charities), benefits checks and local welfare support.
- In England and Wales, the Debt Respite Scheme (Breathing Space), in place since May 2021, gives people in problem debt legal protection from most creditor action: a standard breathing space lasts up to 60 days, and a mental health crisis breathing space lasts for as long as the person is receiving mental health crisis treatment plus 30 days.

Students and doctors
- Many students manage budgets for the first time; financial stress can affect sleep, study and wellbeing.
- Useful habits: a simple budget, knowing your fixed costs, using university hardship and support funds if needed, and seeking advice early rather than borrowing at high interest.
- COM-B applies here too: knowledge (capability), access to advice (opportunity) and habits such as checking spending (automatic motivation).

Exam tips: explain at least two pathways from low income to poor health, state that the debt–mental health relationship is bidirectional, and give concrete actions a clinician can take.

Physical activity is one of the most powerful tools for preventing and treating disease. LMAP-1A uses it as a core theme, including reflection on your own barriers using COM-B.

Definitions
- Physical activity: any bodily movement produced by skeletal muscles that uses energy.
- Exercise: planned, structured, repetitive activity to improve or maintain fitness.
- Sedentary behaviour: waking behaviour with very low energy expenditure while sitting, reclining or lying (about 1.5 METs or less).
- MET (metabolic equivalent): the ratio of energy use during an activity to resting energy use. Commonly used research cut-offs are about 3 to under 6 METs for moderate and 6 or more for vigorous activity; the UK guidelines themselves describe intensity by effort, breathing and heart rate.
- Talk test (used in the UK guidelines): during moderate activity you can talk but not sing; during vigorous activity you have difficulty talking without pausing.

UK Chief Medical Officers' guidelines (updated 10 July 2026)
Published on GOV.UK on 10 July 2026 as an update to the 2019 guidelines. The core adult recommendations are unchanged; changes include allowing the weekly minutes to be built up in bouts of any length (the older adults' 10-minute bout requirement was dropped), stressing that any strengthening activity is better than none, and stating that the evidence does not support a specific numerical limit on sitting time.
- Adults (19–64): be physically active every day; any activity is better than none and more is better still. Do muscle-strengthening activities on at least 2 days a week. Each week accumulate at least 150 minutes of moderate activity (e.g. brisk walking, cycling) or 75 minutes of vigorous activity (e.g. running), or even shorter durations of very vigorous activity (such as sprinting or stair climbing), or a combination, built up in bouts of any length. Minimise sedentary time and break up long periods of inactivity with at least light activity.
- Older adults (65+): as above, plus activities to improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least 2 days a week to reduce falls.
- Children and young people (5–18): an average of at least 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous activity across the week, with a variety of activities that build movement skills, muscle and bone.
- Under-5s: toddlers and pre-schoolers at least 180 minutes a day spread through the day (for 3–4-year-olds including at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity); infants should be active several times a day, including at least 30 minutes of tummy time spread through the day for those not yet mobile.
- Pregnancy and after childbirth: activity is safe and beneficial; vigorous activity is not recommended for previously inactive women.
- The 2026 update also highlights that GLP-1 agonist medicines used for weight management reduce muscle as well as fat, so muscle-strengthening activity is particularly important for them, and it emphasises that even light activity brings some benefit compared with being sedentary.

Physiological benefits
- Cardiovascular: lower resting heart rate, larger stroke volume, lower blood pressure.
- Metabolic: muscle contraction moves GLUT4 to the cell surface independently of insulin, and regular activity improves insulin sensitivity, lowering the risk of type 2 diabetes.
- Musculoskeletal: maintains muscle mass and bone density.
- Mental health: improves mood and sleep and reduces the risk of depression.
- Lower risk of cardiovascular disease, some cancers and dementia; the dose–response curve is steepest at the low end, so the biggest gain comes from moving from inactive to a little active.

Worked example
150 minutes a week can be met by 30 minutes of brisk walking on 5 days, or by 75 minutes of running; one minute of vigorous activity counts roughly as two minutes of moderate activity.

Applying COM-B
Common barriers for students: time (physical opportunity), lack of confidence or skills (capability), and no habit (automatic motivation). Solutions might include active travel, scheduling sessions as fixed appointments, joining a club (social opportunity) and tracking steps (self-monitoring).

Exam tips: quote the adult guideline precisely including the strength component and the sedentary advice, date the guidance (2026 update of the 2019 guidelines), and link benefits to mechanisms.

Nutrition affects almost every chronic disease. You need the UK dietary guidance, how to assess weight, and an honest sense of where the evidence is strong and where it is debated.

Energy and nutrients
- Energy balance: weight changes when intake and expenditure differ over time.
- Energy values used on UK food labels: carbohydrate 4 kcal/g (17 kJ/g), protein 4 kcal/g (17 kJ/g), fat 9 kcal/g (37 kJ/g), alcohol 7 kcal/g (29 kJ/g). 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ.
- Micronutrients include vitamins and minerals; examples of deficiency are iron-deficiency anaemia and vitamin D deficiency (UK advice includes considering a vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter).

The Eatwell Guide (Public Health England, 2016)
- Fruit and vegetables: just over a third of what you eat; at least 5 portions a day.
- Starchy carbohydrates: just over a third; choose wholegrain or higher-fibre versions.
- Some dairy or dairy alternatives (lower-fat, lower-sugar options).
- Beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and other proteins: eat more beans and pulses, 2 portions of fish a week (one oily), and less red and processed meat.
- Small amounts of unsaturated oils and spreads.
- 6–8 cups or glasses of fluid a day.
- Foods high in fat, salt and sugar sit outside the main guide: eat less often and in small amounts.

Specific UK recommendations (from the Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition, SACN)
- Free sugars: no more than 5% of total dietary energy (2015). The NHS translates this as no more than 30 g of free sugars a day for adults. Free sugars are sugars added to food plus those in honey, syrups and unsweetened fruit juices and smoothies, not sugars inside intact fruit, vegetables or milk.
- Fibre: 30 g a day for adults (2015).
- Saturated fat: no more than about 10% of total dietary energy (2019).
- Salt: no more than 6 g a day for adults.

Assessing weight (NICE NG246, overweight and obesity management)
- BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)². Healthy 18.5–24.9; overweight 25–29.9; obesity 30 or more (classes at 30, 35 and 40).
- For people of South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African or African-Caribbean background, lower thresholds apply: overweight from 23 and obesity from 27.5.
- Waist-to-height ratio identifies central adiposity: keep the waist below half of height. 0.5–0.59 indicates increased risk; 0.6 or more, high risk.
- Worked example: 95 kg and 1.75 m → BMI = 95 ÷ 3.0625 ≈ 31.0 (obesity class 1). Waist 96 cm ÷ height 175 cm ≈ 0.55 (increased risk).
- Undernutrition matters too, especially in older and hospitalised people; screening tools such as MUST are used.

Where evidence is debated
- Ultra-processed foods (UPFs): SACN's 2025 rapid evidence update found consistent associations between higher UPF intake and poorer health and considered them concerning, but concluded that causation had not been shown, because the evidence is mostly observational and it is unclear whether harms come from processing itself or from the high energy, saturated fat, salt and sugar content of many such foods.
- The best balance of fat and carbohydrate for weight loss is still debated; overall energy intake and adherence matter more than any single macronutrient pattern for most people.

Population measures
The Soft Drinks Industry Levy (from April 2018) taxes drinks by added sugar content and encouraged manufacturers to reformulate, an example of Rose's population strategy.

Exam tips: quote the Eatwell proportions and SACN figures with dates, calculate BMI and waist-to-height ratio correctly, and signal clearly where evidence is uncertain.

LMAP-1A ends with a summative group assessment. The details below come from Imperial's LMAP pages, which were last updated in 2022, so confirm current arrangements in your 2026-27 module handbook.

What the pages describe (as of 2022)
- In Term 3, students choose one lifestyle medicine theme for deeper study (the pages describe five themes: sleep, nutrition, physical activity, mental health and financial wellbeing).
- Working in teams of 5–6, students produce a short audio podcast (described as five minutes) on real-life approaches to behaviour change in that theme.
- The podcast makes up 80% of the mark; the remainder comes from an individual academic commentary and peer evaluation.

What a strong podcast is likely to show
- Accurate content: correct facts and current UK guidance with dates (e.g. the 2026 update to the UK CMOs' physical activity guidelines, the 2016 low-risk drinking guidelines), and clear signals where evidence is uncertain.
- Behaviour change theory used properly: identify a target behaviour, analyse it with COM-B, and propose named behaviour change techniques that match the barriers you found.
- Evidence: cite good-quality sources (systematic reviews, guidelines) in your commentary, and distinguish association from causation.
- Audience: decide who the podcast is for (patients, students, the public) and pitch language accordingly.
- Inequalities: consider who finds the behaviour hardest to change and why.

Working as a team
- Agree roles early: research, scripting, recording, editing and referencing.
- Set internal deadlines and keep a shared document of sources.
- Peer evaluation rewards fair contribution, so record who did what.

Practical and ethical points
- If you include interviews or personal stories, get informed consent, keep people anonymous unless they agree otherwise, and avoid giving individual medical advice.
- Script first, then record; five minutes is short, so one clear message with a practical takeaway works better than a broad overview.
- Check audio quality: a quiet room and a test recording save time.

The academic commentary
Use it to justify your choices: why this behaviour, which COM-B components you targeted, which techniques you chose and what evidence supports them, and the limitations of your approach.

Exam tips: treat the podcast as applied behaviour change science, not a general talk about a topic; every claim should be checkable and every recommendation tied to a mechanism or technique.

Suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus, entrained by light via the retinohypothalamic tract.
Men and women: safest not to drink more than 14 units a week regularly; if drinking that much, spread it evenly over 3 or more days. Safest not to drink at all in pregnancy.
Units = volume (mL) × ABV (%) ÷ 1,000; e.g. 500 mL at 5% = 2.5 units.
Impaired control; increasing priority of use over other activities; physiological features (tolerance, withdrawal).
McEwen and Stellar (1993): cumulative physiological wear and tear from repeated or chronic stress responses.
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I).
Meta-analysis of 148 studies: stronger social relationships linked to about 50% greater likelihood of survival.
Isolation: objective lack of social contact. Loneliness: subjective feeling that relationships are inadequate.
Cohen and Wills (1985): social support protects health by reducing the impact of stressors.

cards.f: Domestic Abuse Act 2021 definition (England and Wales)
cards.b: Includes physical, sexual, economic, psychological and emotional abuse and controlling or coercive behaviour between personally connected people aged 16+.
"A connected society" (2018), the government's first strategy on loneliness.
Feeling secure and in control: managing day to day, coping with the unexpected, on track for the future.

cards.f: Direction of the debt–mental health link
cards.b: Bidirectional: debt contributes to poor mental health, and mental ill health makes debt more likely.
Debt Respite Scheme since May 2021: standard protection up to 60 days; mental health crisis version lasts for crisis treatment plus 30 days.

cards.f: Three pathways from low income to poor health
cards.b: Material (housing, food), psychosocial (chronic stress, lack of control) and behavioural.
At least 150 min moderate or 75 min vigorous activity a week (or combination), being active every day (UK CMOs, 2026 update).
Muscle-strengthening activities on at least 2 days a week.
Average at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity a day across the week.
Common research cut-offs: moderate about 3 to under 6 METs; vigorous 6 METs or more. The UK guidelines describe intensity by effort and breathing instead.
Moderate: can talk but not sing. Vigorous: difficulty talking without pausing (UK CMOs' guidelines).

cards.f: New emphasis in the 2026 CMO update
cards.b: Muscle-strengthening is especially important for people on GLP-1 agonist weight-loss medicines; light activity still brings some benefit.
Muscle contraction moves GLUT4 to the cell surface independently of insulin; training improves insulin sensitivity.
No more than 5% of total dietary energy (2015); NHS: no more than 30 g a day for adults.
30 g a day (SACN, 2015).
For South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African or African-Caribbean background: overweight from 23, obesity from 27.5.
Keep waist below half of height; 0.5–0.59 increased risk, 0.6+ high risk.

cards.f: Energy per gram on UK labels
cards.b: Carbohydrate 4 kcal, protein 4 kcal, fat 9 kcal, alcohol 7 kcal.
Consistent, concerning associations with poor health, but causation not established; evidence mainly observational.
Podcast 80% of the mark; the rest from an individual academic commentary and peer evaluation.
Teams of 5–6; short audio podcast on real-life behaviour change approaches in one chosen lifestyle theme, in Term 3.

questions.q: In a trial, 10% of the control group and 6% of the treated group have the outcome. What is the number needed to treat?
questions.why: The absolute risk reduction is 0.10 − 0.06 = 0.04, and NNT = 1/0.04 = 25. The answer 4 is the absolute risk reduction in percentage points, not its reciprocal. The answer 40 is the relative risk reduction as a percentage. The answer 17 comes from 1/0.06, using the treated group's risk instead of the difference between groups.

questions.q: A cohort study finds that coffee drinkers have more lung cancer. Later analysis shows coffee drinkers are more likely to smoke. What does this illustrate?
questions.why: Smoking is linked to both coffee drinking and lung cancer, creating a spurious association: this is confounding. Reverse causation would mean lung cancer led people to drink more coffee, which is not suggested. Recall bias arises when cases remember past exposures differently, a problem mainly in case–control designs. Selection bias concerns who enters or stays in the study, not a third factor linked to exposure and outcome.

questions.q: Outline the key ethical requirements for research involving human participants and the historical events that shaped them.
markScheme: Nuremberg Code (1947) after the Nazi doctors' trial: voluntary consent essential
Declaration of Helsinki (WMA, 1964; latest revision October 2024): principles for medical research
Tuskegee study (1932–1972) → Belmont Report (1979): respect for persons, beneficence, justice
Requirements: informed voluntary consent, right to withdraw, confidentiality, favourable risk–benefit balance, fair participant selection
Independent ethics committee review (UK research ethics committees/HRA in England)
questions.modelAnswer: Modern research ethics developed largely in response to abuse. After the trial of Nazi doctors, the Nuremberg Code (1947) made voluntary consent essential. The World Medical Association's Declaration of Helsinki, first adopted in 1964 and most recently revised in October 2024, sets out principles for medical research on people. In the United States, the Tuskegee study (1932–1972), which withheld treatment from Black men with syphilis without informed consent, led to the Belmont Report (1979) and its principles of respect for persons, beneficence and justice. Today researchers must obtain informed, voluntary consent, allow participants to withdraw, protect confidentiality, ensure benefits justify risks, select participants fairly and obtain approval from an independent research ethics committee; in England this is coordinated through the Health Research Authority.

questions.q: In a population, 90% of people are low risk (1% develop a disease) and 10% are high risk (5% develop it). Roughly what share of all cases comes from the low-risk group?
questions.why: Low-risk cases = 0.9 × 0.01 = 0.009; high-risk cases = 0.1 × 0.05 = 0.005; low-risk share = 0.009/0.014 ≈ 64%. This is the prevention paradox. About 36% is the share from the high-risk group, so it answers the opposite question. About 90% is the proportion of people who are low risk, ignoring their lower disease rate. About 10% is the proportion of people who are high risk, confusing population share with share of cases.

questions.q: Which statement describes the inverse care law?
options: Health improves step by step with each rise in social position
The availability of good medical care tends to vary inversely with the need for it
A preventive measure that benefits the population may offer little to each individual
Universal action should be scaled in proportion to disadvantage
questions.why: Julian Tudor Hart's inverse care law (1971) states that good care is least available where need is greatest. Health improving with social position describes the social gradient. Benefit to the population but little to each individual is Rose's prevention paradox. Scaling universal action to disadvantage is the Marmot Review's proportionate universalism.

questions.q: Compare Rose's high-risk and population strategies of prevention, giving an example of each.
markScheme: High-risk strategy: identify individuals at high risk and intervene (e.g. treating people with high blood pressure or high cardiovascular risk)
Advantages: targeted, motivating, good benefit–risk for individuals
Limitations: misses most cases (which arise in the larger lower-risk group); does not address underlying causes; screening costs
Population strategy: shift whole distribution (e.g. salt reduction in processed food, sugar levy)
Advantages: tackles root causes, large total benefit; limitation: small benefit per person (prevention paradox), less individual motivation
questions.modelAnswer: Geoffrey Rose distinguished two approaches. The high-risk strategy identifies people at the top of the risk distribution and intervenes with them, for example offering treatment and lifestyle support to people with high cardiovascular risk. It is well targeted, motivating for patients and clinicians, and gives a favourable balance of benefit and harm for each person. However, because most cases occur among the much larger group at moderate risk, it prevents relatively few cases overall, and it does nothing about why risk is high in the first place. The population strategy aims to shift the whole distribution of a risk factor, for example by reducing salt in processed foods or taxing sugary drinks. It addresses root causes and can prevent many more cases in total, but each individual gains little, so people may see little reason to take part. This is the prevention paradox. In practice the two strategies are complementary.

questions.q: In the COM-B model, a student who lacks time to exercise because of a long commute has a deficit in which component?
questions.why: Time, money, resources and the physical environment are physical opportunity. Psychological capability concerns knowledge and mental skills, which are not the problem here. Reflective motivation concerns plans and beliefs about the behaviour; the student may want to exercise. Social opportunity concerns norms and support from other people, not time.

questions.q: Which statement about the transtheoretical (stages of change) model is most accurate?
options: It was proposed by Michie and colleagues as part of the Behaviour Change Wheel
It has been proven that stage-matched interventions always outperform others
It describes stages from precontemplation to maintenance, but evidence that stage-matched interventions work better is mixed
It has only two stages: intention and action
questions.why: The model (Prochaska and DiClemente) describes precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance, and it is widely taught, but trials have not consistently shown that tailoring interventions to stage improves outcomes. The Behaviour Change Wheel, with COM-B at its centre, comes from Michie and colleagues, so attributing this model to Michie's Behaviour Change Wheel mixes up the two frameworks. Saying stage-matching always works overstates the evidence. The two-stage description leaves out most of the model and resembles intention-based theories instead.

questions.q: A patient says she wants to cut down on sugary drinks but keeps buying them from the vending machine at work. Use COM-B to analyse the behaviour and suggest three specific behaviour change techniques.
markScheme: Capability: likely adequate knowledge (she wants to change), but may lack strategies
Opportunity: physical — vending machine easily available, few alternatives; social — colleagues' habits
Motivation: reflective motivation present; automatic motivation (habit, cravings, cue of the machine) drives behaviour
BCTs matched to barriers, e.g. action planning/prompts, restructuring the environment (carry water, avoid route past machine), self-monitoring, habit replacement/social support
Justifies why techniques target the identified components
questions.modelAnswer: Her capability is probably adequate: she knows the drinks are a problem and wants to change, though she may lack practical strategies. Opportunity is a key barrier: the vending machine is physically convenient and healthier options may be harder to get, and colleagues may also buy drinks, giving a social cue. Her reflective motivation is present, but automatic motivation, meaning habit and cravings triggered by seeing the machine, is driving the behaviour. Suitable techniques target these barriers. First, restructuring the physical environment: bring a refillable water bottle or an alternative drink and avoid walking past the machine. Second, action planning with a habit-replacement plan: 'When I feel like a drink at 3 pm, I will fill my bottle.' Third, self-monitoring: recording drinks bought each day and reviewing progress weekly, possibly with a colleague for social support.

questions.q: A woman drinks a 750 mL bottle of wine at 13.5% ABV. Approximately how many UK units is this?
questions.why: Units = 750 × 13.5 ÷ 1,000 ≈ 10.1, so about 10 units. 7.5 units is what you get by assuming a 'typical' wine strength of 10% (750 × 10 ÷ 1,000) instead of using the 13.5% on the label. 13.5 units simply reads the ABV percentage as the number of units. 101 units comes from dividing by 100 instead of 1,000.

questions.q: Which statement about the UK Chief Medical Officers' low-risk drinking guidelines is correct?
options: Men may drink up to 21 units a week and women 14
It is safest not to drink more than 14 units a week regularly, for both men and women, spread over three or more days
There is a safe daily limit of 4 units for everyone
Drinking small amounts in pregnancy is recommended for health
questions.why: The 2016 guidelines set the same weekly level of 14 units for men and women, and advise that anyone drinking that much should spread it over three or more days. The 21-units-for-men figure comes from the older 1987 weekly guidance (21 for men, 14 for women), which no longer applies. A 'safe daily limit of 4 units' echoes the 1995 daily benchmarks (3 to 4 units for men, 2 to 3 for women), which the 2016 review replaced; the current guidance describes low risk, not a safe level. In pregnancy, or if planning a pregnancy, the advice is that not drinking at all is safest, so recommending small amounts reverses the guidance.

questions.q: Explain the two-process model of sleep regulation and how it accounts for the difficulty of sleeping after a long-haul flight east.
markScheme: Process S: homeostatic sleep pressure rising with time awake (adenosine) and dissipating during sleep
Process C: circadian rhythm from the suprachiasmatic nucleus, entrained by light; melatonin secreted in darkness
Sleep is easiest when high sleep pressure coincides with the circadian sleep phase
After flying east, local bedtime falls during the body's circadian 'wake' phase, so sleep is hard despite sleep pressure
Re-entrainment through light exposure at appropriate times takes several days
questions.modelAnswer: Borbély's two-process model explains sleep timing by two interacting systems. Process S is a homeostatic sleep pressure that builds the longer we are awake (adenosine accumulation contributes) and dissipates during sleep. Process C is the circadian rhythm generated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus, which is entrained by light via the retinohypothalamic tract and promotes wakefulness during the biological day; melatonin is released in darkness. Sleep comes most easily when high sleep pressure coincides with the circadian sleep phase. After flying east, the local bedtime arrives when the body clock is still in its wake-promoting phase, so the traveller struggles to sleep even if tired, then is sleepy in the local morning. The clock gradually re-entrains, helped by morning light at the destination, over several days.

questions.q: Holt-Lunstad and colleagues' 2010 meta-analysis found that stronger social relationships were associated with what?
options: About a 50% greater likelihood of survival
questions.why: The meta-analysis of 148 studies found that people with stronger social relationships had about a 50% greater likelihood of survival (odds ratio about 1.5). The blood pressure figure is not a finding of this study; it confuses a mechanism with the outcome measured. Saying there was no consistent effect contradicts the main finding. The study measured survival, not hospital admissions, so the 'fewer admissions' answer keeps the 50% but attaches it to the wrong outcome.

questions.q: Which best describes loneliness as distinct from social isolation?
options: Having fewer than five social contacts a week
The subjective feeling that one's relationships are inadequate
questions.why: Loneliness is subjective: a person can feel lonely among many people or content with few contacts. Living alone, having few contacts and marital status are objective circumstances, which describe social isolation or living arrangements rather than the feeling of loneliness.

questions.q: Describe two mechanisms by which social relationships may influence physical health, and explain why the evidence is hard to interpret causally.
markScheme: Stress buffering: support reduces the impact of stressors on HPA/sympathetic activation (Cohen and Wills, 1985)
Behavioural/social influence: networks shape norms and support health behaviours, help-seeking and adherence
Evidence mostly observational: confounding (e.g. socioeconomic status, health) cannot be excluded
Reverse causation: illness can reduce social contact
questions.modelAnswer: One mechanism is stress buffering: supportive relationships reduce how threatening stressors feel and how strongly they activate the HPA axis and sympathetic nervous system, which in turn may lower blood pressure, inflammation and sleep disturbance. A second is social influence on behaviour: friends and family shape norms about smoking, drinking, eating and activity, encourage people to seek help, and support adherence to treatment. Interpreting causation is difficult because the evidence is mainly from observational studies. People with strong networks may differ in income, education or baseline health (confounding), and illness itself can shrink social networks, so poor health may cause isolation rather than the reverse.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the evidence on problem debt and mental health?
options: Debt has no association with mental health
The association is strong and runs in both directions
Mental illness protects people from debt
questions.why: Problem debt is strongly associated with depression and anxiety, and the relationship is bidirectional: debt causes stress, and mental ill health can reduce income and make managing money harder. Saying there is no association contradicts consistent evidence. Saying debt 'always' causes depression overstates observational evidence and ignores the reverse direction. The claim that mental illness protects against debt reverses the evidence: mental illness makes debt more likely.

questions.q: A patient in England in problem debt is receiving mental health crisis treatment. Which scheme can protect them from most creditor action during that time?
questions.why: The Debt Respite Scheme (Breathing Space), in force in England and Wales since May 2021, includes a mental health crisis version lasting for the crisis treatment plus 30 days. The Soft Drinks Industry Levy is a tax on sugary drinks. The Domestic Abuse Act 2021 defines and addresses domestic abuse, including economic abuse, but does not pause debts. NICE PH49 is guidance on individual behaviour change, not debt protection.

questions.q: Explain three pathways through which low income can lead to poorer health, and suggest two actions a doctor can take.
markScheme: Material pathway: poor/cold housing, food insecurity, less access to healthy food and safe spaces
Psychosocial pathway: chronic stress, insecurity, lack of control → HPA activation, poor sleep, mental ill health
Behavioural pathway: higher prevalence of smoking and other risk behaviours, often as coping
Action: ask about money worries routinely and sensitively (including in risk assessment)
Action: signpost to free debt advice, benefits checks, local welfare support, Breathing Space; consider social prescribing
questions.modelAnswer: Low income affects health through material conditions: people may live in cold, damp or overcrowded housing, face food insecurity and have less access to healthy food and safe places to be active. It also acts psychosocially: financial insecurity and lack of control cause chronic stress, activating the HPA axis and sympathetic system, disturbing sleep and increasing the risk of anxiety and depression. Finally, there is a behavioural pathway: smoking and some other risk behaviours are more common in deprived groups, often as ways of coping with stress. A doctor can ask, sensitively and routinely, whether money worries are affecting the patient's health, including as part of a mental health risk assessment. They can then signpost to free, independent debt advice, benefits checks and local welfare support, mention protections such as Breathing Space in England and Wales, and use social prescribing link workers where available.

questions.q: According to the UK Chief Medical Officers' guidelines (2026 update), what should adults aged 19–64 aim for each week?
options: At least 150 minutes of moderate or 75 minutes of vigorous activity, plus muscle strengthening on at least 2 days
At least 60 minutes of vigorous activity every day
10,000 steps a day with no strength component
At least 300 minutes of vigorous activity
questions.why: The adult guideline is at least 150 minutes of moderate or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week (or a combination), muscle-strengthening on at least 2 days, and minimising sedentary time. The 60-minutes-a-day figure is the guideline for children and young people (an average of moderate-to-vigorous activity across the week), not adults. A 10,000-step target is popular but is not the UK guideline, and the guideline does include strength. 300 minutes is the top of the 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity range used in WHO guidance, misremembered as a vigorous minimum; the UK vigorous figure is 75 minutes.

questions.q: Why does regular exercise help people with insulin resistance take up glucose into muscle?
options: Exercise increases glucagon, which drives glucose into muscle
Muscle contraction moves GLUT4 to the cell surface by a pathway independent of insulin
Exercise converts fatty acids into glucose in muscle
questions.why: Contraction triggers GLUT4 translocation through insulin-independent signalling, and training also improves insulin sensitivity, so glucose uptake rises even when insulin signalling is impaired. Glucagon acts mainly on the liver to release glucose, not to drive it into muscle. Exercise does not destroy α cells. Fatty acids cannot be turned into net glucose, and muscle does not do gluconeogenesis for export.

questions.q: Using COM-B, analyse why many first-year medical students fall short of the UK physical activity guidelines and propose matched interventions.
markScheme: States the adult guideline (150 min moderate/75 vigorous; strength 2 days; minimise sitting)
Capability: may lack skills/confidence or knowledge of guidelines (psychological/physical)
Opportunity: time pressure, timetable, cost, environment (physical); peer norms (social)
Motivation: competing priorities (reflective); habits of sitting, tiredness (automatic)
Matched BCTs: action planning and scheduling, active travel (environmental restructuring), clubs/buddies (social support), self-monitoring/prompts
questions.modelAnswer: The guideline for adults is at least 150 minutes of moderate or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week, muscle strengthening on two days and minimal sitting. Students may have the physical capability but lack the psychological capability of knowing the guideline or how to fit activity in. Their physical opportunity is limited by long timetables, revision and travel time, and sometimes cost; social opportunity depends on whether peers are active. Reflective motivation competes with academic priorities, and automatic motivation is dominated by sitting habits and tiredness. Interventions should match these barriers: action planning that schedules sessions as fixed appointments; active travel such as walking or cycling to campus, which restructures the routine; joining a club or exercising with a friend for social support; and self-monitoring with step counts plus phone prompts to break up long periods of sitting.

questions.q: A man weighs 95 kg and is 1.75 m tall. What is his BMI and category (general adult thresholds)?
questions.why: BMI = 95 ÷ 1.75² = 95 ÷ 3.0625 ≈ 31.0, which falls in obesity class 1 (30–34.9). 54.3 comes from dividing by height without squaring it (95 ÷ 1.75). 27.1 comes from dividing by 3.5, i.e. doubling the height instead of squaring it. Calling 31.0 'overweight' uses the right number with the wrong category, since overweight is 25–29.9.

questions.q: What is the SACN recommendation for free sugars?
options: No more than 10% of total dietary energy
No more than 5% of total dietary energy
No more than 30% of total dietary energy
Free sugars should be avoided completely
questions.why: SACN (2015) recommended that free sugars should provide no more than 5% of total dietary energy, which the NHS translates as no more than 30 g a day for adults. 10% was the earlier UK limit before 2015 and is also SACN's figure for saturated fat, so it is easily confused. 30% is not a free sugars limit; the '30' comes from the 30 g a day figure. SACN set a ceiling, not complete avoidance.

questions.q: Summarise what UK advisers have concluded about ultra-processed foods and health, and explain why causation is hard to establish.
markScheme: SACN (2023 statement; 2025 rapid evidence update): consistent associations between higher UPF intake and adverse health outcomes, considered concerning
Causation not established
Evidence mainly observational (very few trials) → confounding (e.g. socioeconomic status, BMI) and inconsistent adjustment
Unclear whether harm is due to processing itself or to high energy, saturated fat, salt and free sugars and low fibre in many UPFs
Advice: reduce processed foods high in energy, saturated fat, salt and sugar; follow existing dietary recommendations
questions.modelAnswer: The Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition considered the evidence in a 2023 statement and in a rapid evidence update published in April 2025. It found consistent associations between higher consumption of ultra-processed foods and poorer health outcomes and regarded these associations as concerning. However, it concluded that causation has not been established. The evidence is almost entirely observational, with very few trials, so confounding by factors such as socioeconomic status and body weight is possible and studies adjust for these inconsistently. It is also unclear whether any harm comes from processing itself or from the fact that many such foods are high in energy, saturated fat, salt and free sugars and low in fibre, which are already known to matter. Its practical advice is that most people would benefit from eating fewer processed foods that are high in energy, saturated fat, salt and sugar, in line with existing recommendations.

questions.q: According to Imperial's LMAP pages (last updated 2022), what share of the LMAP-1A summative mark comes from the group podcast?
questions.why: The pages state that the podcast makes up 80% of the mark. 20% is the share that comes from the individual academic commentary and peer evaluation, so it confuses the two parts. 50% assumes an equal split that the pages do not describe. 100% ignores the individual commentary and peer evaluation components.

questions.q: Using the COM-B model and the Behaviour Change Wheel, design an intervention to increase physical activity among first-year medical students. Justify your choices with evidence and explain how you would evaluate the intervention.
markScheme: Defines target behaviour precisely and links to UK CMO guidelines (2026 update): 150 min moderate/75 vigorous, strength 2 days, reduce sitting
Behavioural diagnosis using all COM-B components with plausible student-specific barriers
Selects intervention functions (e.g. enablement, environmental restructuring, education, modelling, incentivisation) matched to the diagnosis
Specifies named BCTs (goal setting, action planning, self-monitoring, feedback, prompts, social support, habit formation) and delivery
Considers policy categories/environment (timetabling, facilities, active travel) and inequalities in access
Evidence: NICE PH49 recommended techniques; habit formation timescales (Lally 2010); acknowledges limits of self-report and stage models
Evaluation: design (e.g. randomised or controlled before-and-after), objective outcome (accelerometer/steps), process measures, follow-up for maintenance, ethics/consent
Coherent structure and critical reflection
questions.modelAnswer:
Target behaviour. The aim is for first-year medical students to meet the UK Chief Medical Officers' guidelines (updated July 2026): at least 150 minutes of moderate or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week, muscle strengthening on at least two days, and less prolonged sitting. A precise, measurable target, such as 'walk or cycle to campus on at least four days a week and attend one strength session', makes design and evaluation easier.

Behavioural diagnosis (COM-B). Physical capability is usually adequate, though some students lack skills or confidence in gyms or sports. Psychological capability may be limited: many do not know the guideline or how little activity brings benefit. Physical opportunity is constrained by long timetables, revision and travel, and sometimes cost. Social opportunity depends on peers; if friends are inactive or socialising centres on sitting, activity is less likely. Reflective motivation may be good in principle but loses out to study priorities. Automatic motivation is shaped by habits of sitting, screen use and tiredness.

Intervention functions and techniques. Enablement and environmental restructuring address opportunity: timetable-friendly sessions near lecture theatres, secure bike storage, and promoting active travel routes. Education addresses knowledge: a short session on the guidelines and the steep early part of the dose–response curve. Modelling and social support address social opportunity: student-led walking groups, clubs and buddy pairs, with visible role models such as clinicians who are active. Specific techniques, in line with NICE PH49 (2014), include goal setting, action planning (when, where and how), self-monitoring with step counts, feedback on progress, phone prompts to break up sitting, and habit formation by attaching activity to existing routines such as the journey to campus. Students should be told that habits take time, with a median of 66 days in Lally and colleagues' 2010 study. Small incentives, such as team challenges, can boost early engagement.

Equity. Students with caring responsibilities, disabilities or financial pressures may face extra barriers, so options should be free, flexible and adaptable.

Evaluation. A randomised design (for example randomising tutorial groups) or a controlled before-and-after study would compare activity between groups. Activity should be measured objectively where possible (accelerometers or phone step data) because self-report overestimates activity. Outcomes should include weekly minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity, strength sessions and sitting time, measured at baseline, at the end of the intervention and at six months to test maintenance. Process measures (attendance, which techniques were used, student feedback) explain why it did or did not work. Participation and data sharing should be voluntary with informed consent, as in LMAP's optional Lifestyle Tracking Study.

Limitations. Volunteers may already be more motivated, and short-term increases often fade; designing for habit and environment rather than relying on information alone gives the best chance of lasting change.

questions.q: "Improving population health depends more on changing social and economic conditions than on persuading individuals to change their behaviour." Discuss.
markScheme: Explains determinants of health (Dahlgren and Whitehead) and the social gradient (Black Report, Marmot 2010)
Uses Rose's population vs high-risk strategies and the prevention paradox, with an example
Evidence on inequalities: Marmot 10 Years On (2020); inverse care law
Argues for individual approaches: behaviour matters, COM-B/BCTs, NICE PH49, clinical brief interventions
Shows that individual behaviour is shaped by opportunity (COM-B) — so the two are linked; risk of 'lifestyle drift' and victim-blaming
Examples of structural interventions: Soft Drinks Industry Levy, smoke-free legislation, housing/income, active travel
Reaches a reasoned conclusion (complementary, proportionate universalism)
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement contrasts two views of prevention: one focused on the conditions in which people live and one on individual choices. The evidence suggests conditions matter most at population level, but the two are closely linked.

The case for social and economic conditions. Dahlgren and Whitehead's model places individual behaviour inside layers of social networks, living and working conditions and wider socio-economic factors. Health follows a social gradient, documented in the Black Report (1980) and the Marmot Review (2010), so differences are not explained by a small group making poor choices. The Marmot Review 10 Years On (2020) reported that improvement in life expectancy had stalled and that inequalities had widened, including falling life expectancy for women in the most deprived areas, pointing to structural causes such as income, housing and education. Rose's prevention paradox shows that most cases arise in the large group at moderate risk, so shifting the whole distribution of a risk factor can prevent more disease than targeting high-risk individuals. Structural measures such as smoke-free legislation and the Soft Drinks Industry Levy (2018), which encouraged reformulation, change behaviour without relying on individual willpower, and they may reduce inequalities because they do not depend on people's resources to act on advice.

The case for individual behaviour change. Behaviours such as smoking, drinking, diet and activity still drive much disease, and individual approaches work for many people. NICE PH49 (2014) recommends interventions built on proven techniques such as goal setting, self-monitoring and social support, and brief advice from clinicians can prompt quit attempts. Individual support is also needed by people who already have risk factors or disease.

Why the dichotomy is false. The COM-B model shows that behaviour depends on opportunity as well as capability and motivation; social and economic conditions largely determine physical and social opportunity. Interventions that rely only on persuasion tend to benefit those with more resources and can widen inequalities, and focusing on individual 'choices' risks blaming people for circumstances outside their control. Conversely, structural change works partly by changing individual behaviour.

Conclusion. At population level, changing social and economic conditions probably achieves more and is fairer, but it should be combined with individual support, scaled to need, as in the Marmot Review's proportionate universalism. The most effective prevention makes healthy behaviour the easy default and supports individuals to use it.
